Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square

derivations.claim: By [L3] choose an ordered orthonormal basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$; replacing $f_0$ by $-f_0$ if necessary we may assume $g_p(f_0,N_p)<0$, so $f_0$ is future-directed and, by [L4] and [L5] as in the rest-space lemma, the future timelike component is $C_p^+=T_+=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and the future causal vectors are the nonzero points of $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$. Write $n=n^0f_0+n_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $w=w^0f_0+w_{\mathrm{vec}}$; then $n^0>\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge0$, $(n^0)^2-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2=1$, and for nonzero future causal $w$ we have $w^0\ge\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ with $w^0>0$ (because $w\neq0$ forces either $\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert>0$ or $w^0>0\ge\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$).

With the coordinates of step 1.1, $g_p(n,w)=-n^0w^0+n_{\mathrm{vec}}\cdot w_{\mathrm{vec}}$, so by [L6] $\gamma(w)=n^0w^0-n_{\mathrm{vec}}\cdot w_{\mathrm{vec}}\ge n^0w^0-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge w^0\bigl(n^0-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\bigr)$. Since $n^0-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert=(n^0+\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert)^{-1}>0$ and $w^0>0$, we get $\gamma(w)>0$; this proves claim 1.

Let $w$ be future unit timelike. By claim 1, $\gamma(w)>0$; by [L2], $g_p(h(w),h(w))=g_p(w,w)+\gamma(w)^2=-1+\gamma(w)^2$, and the left side is $\ge0$ because $h(w)\in n^{\perp}$ and $g_p$ is positive definite there, so $\gamma(w)^2\ge1$ and hence $\gamma(w)\ge1$. Equality holds exactly when $h(w)=0$, i.e. $w\in\ker h=\mathbb Rn$ by [L2]; a future unit timelike vector proportional to $n$ must equal $n$. This proves claim 2.

Let $w$ be unit timelike. It is timelike and nonzero, so by [L5] it is future-directed or past-directed according to membership in $C_p^+$ or $C_p^-$, and $g_p(w,N_p)\neq0$. If $w$ is future-directed, step 2.1 applied to $w$ gives $-g_p(n,w)>0$, i.e. $g_p(n,w)<0$. If $w$ is past-directed, then $-w$ is future unit timelike, so step 2.1 gives $-g_p(n,-w)=g_p(n,w)>0$. Conversely, if $g_p(n,w)<0$ and $w$ were past-directed, the previous case would give $g_p(n,w)>0$, a contradiction; and if $g_p(n,w)>0$ and $w$ were future-directed, the first case would give $g_p(n,w)<0$, a contradiction. Hence $w$ is future-directed exactly when $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed exactly when $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular $g_p(n,w)\neq0$. This proves claim 3.
Claims 1, 2 and 3 are steps 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2 respectively.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The map $h$ is linear because $v\mapsto g_p(n,v)$ is linear and $n$ is fixed. Moreover $h(n)=n+g_p(n,n)n=n-n=0$, and if $v\in n^{\perp}$ then $g_p(n,v)=0$ and $h(v)=v$; hence for every $v$ one has $g_p(h(v),n)=g_p(v,n)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,n)=g_p(v,n)-g_p(v,n)=0$, so $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$, and then $h(h(v))=h(v)+g_p(h(v),n)n=h(v)$, that is, $h\circ h=h$.

By [L2] choose an ordered $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$. The vector $f_0$ is timelike, and [L4] gives $g_p(f_0,N_p)\neq0$; replacing $f_0$ by $-f_0$ if necessary, which preserves orthonormality, we may assume $g_p(f_0,N_p)<0$, so that $f_0\in C_p^+$ and $f_0$ is future-directed. By [L3] the two components of the timelike set are $T_+=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and $T_-=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ in this basis, in some order; since $f_0$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)\in T_+$ and lies in $C_p^+$, the identification is $C_p^+=T_+$. Writing $n=n^0f_0+n^1f_1+n^2f_2+n^3f_3$ by [L6] and using that $n$ is future unit timelike, we get $n^0>\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge0$ and $(n^0)^2-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2=1$.

From $h(v)=0$ we get $v=-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$, and conversely $h(n)=0$, so $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$; since $h$ fixes every vector of $n^{\perp}$ pointwise and its image lies in $n^{\perp}$, its image is exactly $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$.

Using bilinearity and symmetry of $g_p$, $g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v+g_p(n,v)n,\,w+g_p(n,w)n)=g_p(v,w)+g_p(n,w)g_p(v,n)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)g_p(n,n)$, and the last term is $-g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$ because $g_p(n,n)=-1$; hence $g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$. Taking $w=v$ gives the stated special case.

Let $v\in n^{\perp}$, with coordinates $v=v^0f_0+v_{\mathrm{vec}}$ as in step 1.2. Since $0=g_p(v,n)=-v^0n^0+v_{\mathrm{vec}}\cdot n_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $n^0\ge1>0$ by step 1.2, we have $v^0=(v_{\mathrm{vec}}\cdot n_{\mathrm{vec}})/n^0$, and by [L7] $\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\cdot n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\,\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$; therefore $g_p(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2(1-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2/(n^0)^2)=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\bigl((n^0)^2-\lvert n_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\bigr)/(n^0)^2=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2/(n^0)^2\ge0$. Equality forces $\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert=0$ and then $v^0=0$, that is, $v=0$. Hence $g_p$ is positive definite on $n^{\perp}$.

The displayed formula $v=-g_p(v,n)n+h(v)$ is a rearrangement of the definition of $h$, and the two summands lie in $\mathbb Rn$ and $n^{\perp}$. If $v=\lambda n+w$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and $w\in n^{\perp}$, then applying $g_p(\cdot,n)$ gives $g_p(v,n)=-\lambda$, so $\lambda=-g_p(v,n)$ and $w=v+g_p(v,n)n=h(v)$; hence the decomposition is unique and $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$. It is orthogonal because $g_p(\lambda n,w)=\lambda g_p(n,w)=0$ for $w\in n^{\perp}$, and $\mathbb Rn\cap n^{\perp}=\{0\}$ since $g_p(\lambda n,n)=-\lambda$ vanishes only for $\lambda=0$.

The vectors $h(f_1),h(f_2),h(f_3)$ lie in $n^{\perp}$ by step 1.1 and are linearly independent: if $\sum_ic^ih(f_i)=0$, then $h(\sum_ic^if_i)=0$, so $\sum_ic^if_i\in\mathbb Rn$ by step 2.1. This vector has zero first coordinate in the basis of step 1.2, while a vector $\lambda n$ has first coordinate $\lambda n^0$ with $n^0>0$. Hence $\lambda=0$ and all $c^i=0$ by [L6]. The four vectors $n,h(f_1),h(f_2),h(f_3)$ are linearly independent: pairing a linear relation with $n$ first makes the coefficient of $n$ zero, and the just-proved independence makes the others zero. Since $T_pM$ has dimension $4$, they form a basis. For $v\in n^{\perp}$, expand in this basis and pair with $n$ again; the coefficient of $n$ is zero. Thus the three projected spatial vectors span $n^{\perp}$ and form its basis, giving dimension $3$. Together with step 2.3 this proves claim 3 without assuming the generic basis vector $f_0$ equals $n$ or $h(f_0)=0$.
Claims 1 and 2 are steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 2.2, and claim 3 is steps 2.3 and 3.2.

The zero vector satisfies $h(0)=0$, $0=-g_p(0,n)n+h(0)$ and lies in $\ker h$; steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 include it, and positive definiteness of $g_p$ on $n^{\perp}$ has equality only at $v=0$ by step 2.3.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $r,s\ge0$ be integers.

**(a) Tensors at a point.** For $p\in M$, the tangent space $T_pM$ is the real
vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]) and the cotangent space is
its algebraic dual, $T_p^*M=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]). A **type
$(r,s)$ tensor at $p$** is a multilinear map

$$T_p:(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\longrightarrow\mathbb R,$$

in the sense of [[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]:
the first $r$ arguments are covectors and the last $s$ are vectors. In
particular a type $(1,0)$ tensor is a vector, a type $(0,1)$ tensor is a
covector and a type $(0,2)$ tensor is a bilinear form, so the covariant
$2$-tensors of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] are exactly the
type $(0,2)$ tensors of this definition.

**(b) The tensor bundle and smooth fields.** The **type $(r,s)$ tensor bundle**
$T^r_sM$ is the disjoint union of the fibres $T^r_sM|_p=\operatorname{Mult}((T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s,\mathbb R)$
over $p\in M$ ([[def-type-r-s-tensor-bundle]]); it carries the smooth
vector-bundle structure defined by the tensor-coordinate change rules
([[lem-gr-tensor-bundle-coordinate-construction]]). A **smooth
tensor field of type $(r,s)$** on $M$ is a family $T=(T_p)_{p\in M}$ assigning
to each $p$ a type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$, such that for every smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas the **component functions**

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}(q):=T_q\bigl(dx^{a_1}|_q,\dots,dx^{a_r}|_q,\ \partial_{b_1}|_q,\dots,\partial_{b_s}|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$; here the coordinate derivations
$\partial_b|_q=\partial/\partial x^b|_q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]) and the
coordinate differentials $dx^a|_q$ form the dual basis of $T_q^*M$
([[thm-coordinate-differentials-form-the-dual-cotangent-basis]]). This is
equivalent to $T$ being a smooth section of $T^r_sM$ in the sense of
[[def-smooth-tensor-field]]: the component functions are the frame
coefficients of the section in the local frame induced by the chart. The
smoothness condition is independent of the chosen smooth atlas and the
components in two overlapping charts are related by the transformation law
proved in the lemma on this page; the definition is therefore chart
independent rather than merely chart-wise.

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices are written $a,b,c,\dots$ for components in
a chart, with the Einstein summation convention: a repeated index, once upper
and once lower, is summed over $0,1,2,3$. An upper index is a contravariant
slot in which a covector is evaluated, a lower index a covariant slot in which
a vector is evaluated. Slots are moved between these positions with the
musical isomorphisms $\flat_p,\sharp_p$ of
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] to change slot variance.
For example, if $T$ is a type $(1,1)$ field, lowering its contravariant slot
gives the type $(0,2)$ field with components $T_{ab}:=g_{ac}T^c{}_b$; if $S$
is a type $(0,2)$ field, raising its first covariant slot gives the type
$(1,1)$ field with components $S^a{}_b:=g^{ac}S_{cb}$. Each operation changes
the tensor type and is invertible because $g_p$ is nondegenerate.

**(d) Scope.** The definition is purely local and chart-based; no global
triviality of $T^r_sM$, no global frame and no choice of metric-compatible
fields is assumed or implied. All fields are smooth ($C^\infty$); no
lower-regularity or distributional tensor field is defined here. The smooth
structure of the tangent bundle, and hence of $T^r_sM$
([[lem-gr-tensor-bundle-coordinate-construction]]), inherits the
axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] recorded with
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the component formulation of smoothness
itself makes no choice.

Let $(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ be smooth charts on $M$ with $p\in U\cap V$. Then
$$ \partial_{x^i}|_p=\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial (y^j\circ x^{-1})}{\partial x^i}(x(p))\,\partial_{y^j}|_p $$
for each $i$.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart around $p$, then the covectors $dx^1_p,\dots,dx^n_p$ form the basis of $T_p^*M$ dual to the tangent basis $\partial_{x^1}|_p,\dots,\partial_{x^n}|_p$.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.
For every smooth chart $(U,x)$ containing $p$, each coordinate operator $\partial_i|_p$ from [[def-coordinate-derivations-at-a-point]] is a well-defined derivation at $p$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $q\in\mathbb N_0$, let $W\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and
let $f:W\to\mathbb R^q$. The map $f$ is **smooth** (of class $C^\infty$) when
every component $f_l:W\to\mathbb R$, $l<q$, is of class $C^k$ for
every $k\in\mathbb N$, where scalar
$C^k$ means that every iterated coordinate derivative through order $k$ exists
and is continuous on $W$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).
For $m=0$ the domain is the one-point space or the empty set and every map from
it is declared smooth; for $q=0$ there are no components and every map into the
one-point space is smooth.

Let $M$ be a topological $n$-manifold and let $(U,\varphi)$ and $(V,\psi)$ be
charts on $M$ ([[def-manifold-chart-coordinate-domain-and-coordinate-functions]]).
The charts are **smoothly compatible** when $U\cap V=\varnothing$, or when
$n\ge1$ and both **transition maps**

$$\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U\cap V)\longrightarrow\psi(U\cap V), \qquad \varphi\circ\psi^{-1}:\psi(U\cap V)\longrightarrow\varphi(U\cap V)$$

are smooth in the sense above. Both directions of the transition are part of the
definition; in dimension zero overlapping charts have the same one-point image,
the only transition is the identity, and overlapping charts are declared
compatible.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.
Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $r\in\mathbb N$. If the entries of $A:U\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ are $C^r$ and $\det A$ never vanishes, then the entries of $A^{-1}$ are $C^r$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

derivations.claim: Fix $q\in U\cap V$ and write $\partial_{x^i}:=\partial_{x^i}|_q$, $\partial_{y^j}:=\partial_{y^j}|_q$, $dx^i:=dx^i|_q$, $dy^j:=dy^j|_q$. By [L2] applied to the two charts, $\partial_{y^{b}}=\sum_{d}\frac{\partial x^{d}}{\partial y^{b}}(y(q))\,\partial_{x^{d}}$. By [L3] and [L4], $dy^{a}$ is the dual basis element of $\partial_{y^{a}}$ and its coefficients in the dual basis $(dx^c)$ are $dy^{a}(\partial_{x^{c}})=\partial_{x^{c}}(y^{a})=\frac{\partial y^{a}}{\partial x^{c}}(x(q))$; hence $dy^{a}=\sum_{c}\frac{\partial y^{a}}{\partial x^{c}}(x(q))\,dx^{c}$.

Since $T_q$ is multilinear in its $r$ covector and $s$ vector arguments, substituting the expansions of step 1.1 into the definition of the $y$-components gives the displayed transformation law: each contravariant slot contributes one factor $\frac{\partial y^{a_i}}{\partial x^{c_i}}(x(q))$ and each covariant slot one factor $\frac{\partial x^{d_j}}{\partial y^{b_j}}(y(q))$, and the sums over the intermediate indices are finite.

In the special case $r=s=0$ the double sum is empty and the law reduces to $T'(y(q))=T(x(q))$; in the case $r=1,s=0$ it reduces to the vector transformation law and in the case $r=0,s=1$ to the covector law of step 1.1.

Suppose $T$ has $C^\infty$ components in the charts of one smooth atlas $\mathcal A$. Let $(V,y)$ be any smooth chart and $q\in V$; choose a chart $(U,x)$ of $\mathcal A$ with $q\in U$ (the charts of $\mathcal A$ cover $M$). By step 2.1 the components of $T$ in $y$ equal the finite sum of step 2.1, whose factors are: the numbers computed from the components of $T$ in $x$, which are $C^\infty$ functions of $x$ by hypothesis, evaluated along the smooth map $x$; and the Jacobian entries $\frac{\partial y^{a}}{\partial x^{c}}\circ x$ and $\frac{\partial x^{d}}{\partial y^{b}}\circ y$, which are $C^\infty$ on the overlap by [L5] and [L6]. By [L7] the sum is $C^\infty$ on $y(U\cap V)$. Since $q$ and $(V,y)$ were arbitrary, the components of $T$ are $C^\infty$ in every smooth chart, so $T$ is a smooth tensor field by [L1]. The converse direction is immediate from [L1], since the maximal atlas contains every smooth atlas.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove the transformation law and step 3.2 proves the smoothness criterion.

boundaries.evidence: Each point $q\in U\cap V$ is treated separately in step 2.1, so the identity is vacuous on an empty overlap; the smoothness criterion of step 3.2 also covers the case where the sum defining $T'$ is empty (r=s=0), reducing the law to $T'(y(q))=T(x(q))$ as recorded in step 3.1.
The zero tensor field has all components zero and satisfies the law with both sides zero; steps 2.1 and 3.1 use no invertibility or nonvanishing hypothesis, so the zero case is included.
The cases $r+s=1$ are the vector and covector laws computed explicitly in step 1.1 and isolated in step 3.1; the general product formula reduces to the single Jacobian factor there.

boundaries.reason: No nondegeneracy is assumed or needed: the transformation law is a multilinear identity in the components and the smoothness transfer uses only finiteness and smoothness of the sums.
All chart domains are open subsets of a manifold without boundary and every statement is local at a point, so no interval endpoint or limiting parameter occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.2 fixes one arbitrary smooth chart $(V,y)$, one point $q$ and one chart of the given atlas containing $q$; this is a single existential instantiation in a pointwise argument, and no infinite family of choices is made.
The forward direction of the smoothness criterion is step 3.2's hypothesis: smoothness of the components in the charts of one smooth atlas is assumed and shown to propagate to every smooth chart.

The converse direction, smoothness in every smooth chart implies smoothness in the charts of the given atlas, is immediate from the maximal atlas containing every smooth atlas, as stated in the final sentence of step 3.2.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open subset
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$\eta:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ for the four-by-four diagonal matrix with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, and use capital indices $A,B=0,1,2,3$ for frame
members.

**(a) Local frame fields.** A **local frame field** on $U$ is a tuple
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of smooth vector fields on $U$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that for every
$q\in U$ the vectors $E_0(q),E_1(q),E_2(q),E_3(q)$ form an ordered basis of
$T_qM$, equivalently a pointwise independent tuple of four vector fields.

**(b) Coordinate frames.** If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart, the tuple
$(\partial/\partial x^0,\partial/\partial x^1,\partial/\partial x^2,\partial/\partial x^3)$
of coordinate fields is a local frame field on $U$, its **coordinate frame**.
Two coordinate fields of one chart commute: by the coordinate formula for the
Lie bracket ([[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]],
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]) applied to constant coordinate
components, $[\partial/\partial x^a,\partial/\partial x^b]=0$ for all $a,b$.
Consequently a local frame field $(E_0,\dots,E_3)$ with $[E_A,E_B]\neq0$ for
some $A,B$ is not the coordinate frame of any chart; this necessary condition
is the only one asserted here, and no converse is claimed by this definition.

**(c) Tetrad fields.** A **tetrad field** (or **$g$-orthonormal frame field**)
on $U$ is a local frame field $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$ such that

$$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\eta_{AB}\qquad\text{for all }A,B\text{ and all }q\in U .$$

A tetrad field is **future-directed** when in addition $E_0(q)$ is
future-directed for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]); then
each $E_0(q)$ is an observer at $q$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so
$E_0$ is an observer congruence on $U$
([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]), while $E_1,E_2,E_3$ are pointwise an
orthonormal basis of the rest space of that observer. Neither existence of a
tetrad field on a prescribed open set, nor global existence on $M$, is
asserted by this definition; local existence near every point is proved in the
existence theorem on this page.

**(d) Observer-adapted tetrads.** Given an observer $n$ at a point $p$, a
tetrad at $p$ is **$n$-adapted** when its first member is $n$. Given an
observer congruence $n$ on $U$, a tetrad field on $U$ is
**$n$-adapted** when $E_0=n$; its remaining members are then $g$-orthonormal
fields in the moving rest spaces of the congruence.

**(e) Scope.** A tetrad field is not assumed to be a coordinate frame, and a
frame field is not assumed to be orthonormal. Components of a tensor field in a
tetrad and components in a chart are different objects; the transformation
rules for the two are distinguished later on this page. No relation to the
physical interpretation of a reference frame is asserted here beyond the
geometric data listed above.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $r,s\ge0$ be integers.

**(a) Tensors at a point.** For $p\in M$, the tangent space $T_pM$ is the real
vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]) and the cotangent space is
its algebraic dual, $T_p^*M=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]). A **type
$(r,s)$ tensor at $p$** is a multilinear map

$$T_p:(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\longrightarrow\mathbb R,$$

in the sense of [[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]:
the first $r$ arguments are covectors and the last $s$ are vectors. In
particular a type $(1,0)$ tensor is a vector, a type $(0,1)$ tensor is a
covector and a type $(0,2)$ tensor is a bilinear form, so the covariant
$2$-tensors of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] are exactly the
type $(0,2)$ tensors of this definition.

**(b) The tensor bundle and smooth fields.** The **type $(r,s)$ tensor bundle**
$T^r_sM$ is the disjoint union of the fibres $T^r_sM|_p=\operatorname{Mult}((T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s,\mathbb R)$
over $p\in M$ ([[def-type-r-s-tensor-bundle]]); it carries the smooth
vector-bundle structure defined by the tensor-coordinate change rules
([[lem-gr-tensor-bundle-coordinate-construction]]). A **smooth
tensor field of type $(r,s)$** on $M$ is a family $T=(T_p)_{p\in M}$ assigning
to each $p$ a type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$, such that for every smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas the **component functions**

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}(q):=T_q\bigl(dx^{a_1}|_q,\dots,dx^{a_r}|_q,\ \partial_{b_1}|_q,\dots,\partial_{b_s}|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$; here the coordinate derivations
$\partial_b|_q=\partial/\partial x^b|_q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]) and the
coordinate differentials $dx^a|_q$ form the dual basis of $T_q^*M$
([[thm-coordinate-differentials-form-the-dual-cotangent-basis]]). This is
equivalent to $T$ being a smooth section of $T^r_sM$ in the sense of
[[def-smooth-tensor-field]]: the component functions are the frame
coefficients of the section in the local frame induced by the chart. The
smoothness condition is independent of the chosen smooth atlas and the
components in two overlapping charts are related by the transformation law
proved in the lemma on this page; the definition is therefore chart
independent rather than merely chart-wise.

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices are written $a,b,c,\dots$ for components in
a chart, with the Einstein summation convention: a repeated index, once upper
and once lower, is summed over $0,1,2,3$. An upper index is a contravariant
slot in which a covector is evaluated, a lower index a covariant slot in which
a vector is evaluated. Slots are moved between these positions with the
musical isomorphisms $\flat_p,\sharp_p$ of
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] to change slot variance.
For example, if $T$ is a type $(1,1)$ field, lowering its contravariant slot
gives the type $(0,2)$ field with components $T_{ab}:=g_{ac}T^c{}_b$; if $S$
is a type $(0,2)$ field, raising its first covariant slot gives the type
$(1,1)$ field with components $S^a{}_b:=g^{ac}S_{cb}$. Each operation changes
the tensor type and is invertible because $g_p$ is nondegenerate.

**(d) Scope.** The definition is purely local and chart-based; no global
triviality of $T^r_sM$, no global frame and no choice of metric-compatible
fields is assumed or implied. All fields are smooth ($C^\infty$); no
lower-regularity or distributional tensor field is defined here. The smooth
structure of the tangent bundle, and hence of $T^r_sM$
([[lem-gr-tensor-bundle-coordinate-construction]]), inherits the
axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] recorded with
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the component formulation of smoothness
itself makes no choice.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty
open subset, carrying the restricted smooth structure of
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field
$n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that
$n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly,

$$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$

Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing. A single observer
at a point is therefore not a congruence, and a congruence is not an ordered
basis or frame of $T_qM$.

**(b) Observer curves.** Because $n$ is a smooth vector field on $U$, the
theorem on maximal integral curves
([[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]],
[[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]) assigns to every $q\in U$ a unique
maximal integral curve $\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$,
defined on an open interval $I_q\subseteq\mathbb R$. We call these curves the
**observers** (or **observer curves**) of the congruence. Each curve is regular:
for every $s\in I_q$, $\gamma_q'(s)=n_{\gamma_q(s)}$ and

$$g_{\gamma_q(s)}\bigl(n_{\gamma_q(s)},n_{\gamma_q(s)}\bigr)=-1,$$

so its tangent is nonzero, unit timelike and future-directed. Completeness of
the maximal intervals $I_q$, and global product or foliation structure of
$U$, are not asserted. The parameter $s$ is the flow parameter of $n$; it is
not identified with any clock reading here.

**(c) Adapted charts.** An **$n$-adapted chart** is a smooth chart
$(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U'\to\mathbb R^4$ of $M$ whose domain $U'$ is a nonempty
open subset of $U$ and whose **spatial coordinates** $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant
along every integral curve $\gamma:J\to U'$ of the restricted field
$n|_{U'}$, where $J$ is an interval. Equivalently, for each maximal observer
curve $\gamma_q:I_q\to U$, each connected component $K$ of
$\gamma_q^{-1}(U')$ (a maximal nonempty interval contained in this open
subset of $\mathbb R$), and $i=1,2,3$, the function
$u^i\circ\gamma_q$ is constant on $K$. If $q\in U'$ and $0\in K$, this
constant is $u^i(q)$. This condition does not identify labels on different
components when a maximal curve leaves and re-enters $U'$. No global adapted
chart, and no adapted chart on all of $U$, is
asserted by this definition; one exists near every point of $U$ by the
existence corollary proved on this page.

**(d) Scope.** A congruence is a field of observer directions on an open set; it
is not a chart, not a tetrad field, and not a family of parametrized
worldlines with specified domains. The physical reading of its observer curves
as ideal-clock worldlines, and the identification of the flow parameter with a
measurable time, belong to the physical postulates of the framework and are not
asserted here.

Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$, and let $X$ be a vector
field on $U$. Then $X$ is smooth if and only if there exist smooth functions
$X^1,\dots,X^n:U\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} $$

on $U$.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

Let $p \mapsto \mathcal D_p \subseteq T_pM$ be a rank-$k$ family of tangent
subspaces on a smooth manifold $M$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $\mathcal D$ is a smooth distribution.
2. Every point of $M$ has a neighborhood $U$ and smooth vector fields
   $X_1,\dots,X_k$ on $U$ such that the vectors $X_1(q),\dots,X_k(q)$ are
   linearly independent and span $\mathcal D_q$ for all $q \in U$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries the canonical smooth vector
bundle structure supplied by
[[thm-the-tangent-bundle-has-a-canonical-smooth-2n-manifold-structure]]. Let
$M$ be a smooth manifold and let $k \geq 0$ be an integer. A
**smooth distribution of rank $k$ on $M$** is a rank-$k$ smooth vector
subbundle $\mathcal D \subseteq TM$.

Equivalently, to each $p \in M$ it assigns a $k$-dimensional linear subspace
$\mathcal D_p \subseteq T_pM$, with the dependence on $p$ smooth in the sense
of vector subbundles.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
For a nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$, the hyperplane distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$.

A smooth distribution $\mathcal D$ on $M$ is **involutive** when

$$ X,Y \in \Gamma(\mathcal D) \implies [X,Y] \in \Gamma(\mathcal D). $$

That is, the smooth vector fields tangent to $\mathcal D$ are closed under the
Lie bracket.

Let $\mathcal D$ be a rank-$k$ smooth distribution on an $n$-manifold $M$. Then
the following are equivalent:

1. $\mathcal D$ is integrable.
2. $\mathcal D$ is involutive.

When these conditions hold, every point $p \in M$ has a coordinate
neighborhood $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ in which
